# Baruch Chapter 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Baruch 1 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/BAR_001_page_001.jpg

---

**1** This is the book that Baruch wrote in Babylon — Baruch, who was the son of Neriah, grandson of Mahseiah, great-grandson of Zedekiah, who came from Hasadiah, who came from Hilkiah.

**2** He wrote it in the fifth year after Jerusalem fell, on the seventh day of the month — the year the Chaldeans marched in and burned the city to the ground.

**3** Baruch read the whole book aloud to Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, the exiled king of Judah, and to everyone who had gathered to hear it —

**4** the powerful men of the community, the sons of the royal family, the community elders, and all the people, high and low alike, every Judean living beside the River Sud in Babylon.

**5** When he finished reading, they all wept. They fasted and prayed to the Lord.

**6** Then they took up a collection, each person giving what they could afford,

**7** and they sent the money back to Jerusalem — to the high priest Jehoiakim son of Hilkiah son of Shallum, to the other priests, and to all the people still living there.

**8** This was the same occasion when Jehoiakim received back the sacred vessels that had been looted from the temple — he was returning them to the land of Judah on the tenth of Sivan. These were the silver vessels that King Zedekiah son of Josiah had made,

**9** after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had torn Jeconiah and the royal court and the prisoners of war and the soldiers and the common people away from Jerusalem and marched them off to Babylon.

**10** The message they sent said: Here is money. Use it to buy burnt offerings, sin offerings, incense, and grain offerings, and put them all on the altar of the Lord our God.

**11** Pray for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and for his son Belshazzar. Ask that they may live as long as the heavens last.

**12** If the Lord is with us, he will give us strength and open our eyes. We will live under the shelter of Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar, serve them for many years, and win their goodwill.

**13** But also pray for us to the Lord our God, because we have sinned against him. His anger has not cooled toward us, not even now.

**14** Read this book aloud in the temple on the festival days and at every appointed season, as a public confession of sin.

**15** When you read it, say this: The Lord our God is in the right. We are the ones who should be ashamed — we who live in Judah and Jerusalem,

**16** we and our kings, our leaders, our priests, our prophets, and our ancestors before us.

**17** We sinned against the Lord.

**18** We defied him. We refused to listen to his voice. We did not walk in the ways he had laid out for us.

**19** From the day he rescued our ancestors from Egypt right down to today, we have been a disobedient people. We have ignored the Lord our God; we have been careless with his voice.

**20** That is why all the disasters he threatened through his servant Moses have caught up with us. The curse has come true. On the very day he led our ancestors out of Egypt to give them this land — a land of milk and honey — he warned what would happen if we turned away. And it has all come upon us, just as he said.

**21** We have not listened to the Lord our God. We have not heeded the prophets he sent us, one after another.

**22** Every one of us has gone chasing after the desires of an evil heart. We have worshipped other gods and done everything the Lord our God calls evil.

---
*PNEUMA notes: The chapter establishes the scene with emotional weight — a community of exiles weeping by the rivers of Babylon. The awkward political prayer for Nebuchadnezzar (vv.11-12) is retained but framed as pragmatic survival theology, not endorsement. The confessional rhythm in vv.15-22 is rendered with accumulating force.*
